claims.text: Silicon doping of boride-based components promotes in situ formation of an aluminosilicate barrier during exposure to molten aluminum.
The resulting aluminosilicate barrier is thin and adherent.
The aluminosilicate barrier reduces corrosion by limiting direct attack of molten aluminum on the boride matrix.
Standard boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment lack targeted compositional modifications.
Approximately 660°C is a typical hot-dip aluminum-plating temperature.
Silicon segregates to the component surface at high temperature.
Surface silicon reacts with aluminum from the molten bath to form an aluminosilicate layer.
The aluminosilicate layer is stable under the proposed exposure conditions.
The aluminosilicate layer passivates the surface by decreasing contact between molten aluminum and the boride matrix.
Decreasing contact between molten aluminum and the boride matrix mitigates matrix dissolution and corrosion.
Silicon-treated components will exhibit less weight loss than untreated components under identical hot-dip conditions.
Silicon-treated components will exhibit shallower corrosion penetration than untreated components.
Silicon-treated components will exhibit less surface degradation than untreated components.
The intervention should remain effective when silicon concentration is within a controlled range and temperature remains near 660°C.
Extreme thermal cycling or contamination may undermine the barrier's integrity.
Similar barrier-forming mechanisms have been observed in other high-temperature alloy systems.
The behavior of silicon dopants in boride matrices exposed to molten aluminum is not well established.
